claims.text: Prolonged high-temperature annealing enhances atomic intermixing in HEA nanoparticles.
Enhanced intermixing reduces the tendency of Cu and Pd to segregate to nanoparticle surfaces.
Uniform atomic mixing preserves a single solid-solution phase.
Annealing-induced uniform mixing maintains structural and chemical stability throughout 473–1923 K.
Initially solid-solution HEA nanoparticles may contain slight atomic inhomogeneities.
Annealing near 1923 K for a sufficient duration can overcome kinetic diffusion barriers and produce complete atomic mixing.
An inert or controlled atmosphere minimizes external oxidation or contamination during operation.
Enhanced atomic interdiffusion produces a uniformly mixed single-phase solid solution.
High-temperature treatment increases atomic mobility and enables atoms to overcome local energy barriers.
Cu and Pd have lower cohesive energies that drive their surface segregation.
Uniform redistribution reduces the thermodynamic driving force for surface segregation by lower-cohesive-energy elements.
Annealed nanoparticles will retain a stable lattice with little secondary-phase formation or elemental segregation.
Untreated particles will develop more surface-compositional variation or segregated phases than annealed particles under the same operating conditions.
As-synthesized nanoparticles without prolonged annealing undergo measurable segregation and phase instability during extended high-temperature operation.
Insufficient annealing temperature or duration can fail to produce full homogenization.
Annealing that induces melting or unwanted grain growth falls outside the conditions under which the prediction should hold.
The optimum annealing duration and temperature profile vary with the diffusion kinetics of the constituent metals.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis asserts that annealing and uniform redistribution minimize Cu and Pd surface segregation, but cited record PMC11247481::web::010::surface_stability reports pronounced equilibrium segregation of Cu and Pd to the surface after high-temperature annealing.
